system_description.narrative_title: AI governance shock, market stress and geopolitical fracture
system_description.narrative_summary: The global order is an open, tightly coupled system in flux where a corporate governance crisis in the AI sector cascades into markets, trade policy and great‑power rivalry even as inflation, bond yields and energy shocks test policy space. Simultaneously, regional conflicts (Ukraine, Middle East) and climate/energy transitions create cross‑cutting pressures that force states and firms to reconfigure alliances, supply chains and regulatory regimes. The result is heightened systemic sensitivity: small shocks in tech or energy produce large, distributed consequences across finance, security and diplomacy.
system_description.scope: States and coalitions, multinational corporations (notably tech and energy firms), global financial markets and central banks, supply chains and export controls, regional conflicts, international institutions, and public and investor sentiment that link these actors.
system_description.super_system: The international political‑economic system (the global order of interdependent states, markets and transnational institutions).
adjacent_subsystems: Global financial markets and central banking
US‑China high‑technology competition and export‑control regime
Energy security and Middle East geopolitics
Regional conflict and European security (Ukraine, NATO, Russia)

variables.name: US–China tech and AI export rivalry
variables.description: The United States and China are contesting control of advanced semiconductor and AI supply chains as tighter U.S. export curbs and Chinese efforts to secure or circumvent them reshape technological competition.

variables.name: Russia–Ukraine war and stalled diplomacy
variables.description: Russia, Ukraine and their external backers remain locked in high-intensity conflict with episodic negotiations, prisoner swaps and no durable settlement, producing shifting frontlines and fraught diplomacy.

variables.name: Iran regional confrontation and maritime attacks
variables.description: Iran, regional states, U.S. forces and proxy actors are engaged in escalating low- and mid-intensity strikes — including attacks on shipping and energy infrastructure — alongside a parallel nuclear and diplomatic standoff that raises wider instability.

variables.name: European security realignment and alliance strain
variables.description: European governments, NATO partners and the United States are renegotiating burden‑sharing, leadership and diplomatic posture in European security as debates grow over greater European agency and how to handle Russia.

variables.name: Global monetary tightening and market stress
variables.description: Major central banks, global financial markets and governments are shifting toward tighter monetary policy amid persistent inflation, rising yields and asset repricing, raising systemic risks across bond, equity and credit markets.
